extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners evaluating nature-based product eligibility)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the "markedly different characteristics" comparison when evaluating whether a claimed nature-based product is a judicially-excepted "product of nature" for patent-eligibility (Step 2A analysis). Covers when to apply the test, how to select counterparts and characteristics, and how to judge whether differences are "marked."

rubrics_metrics.name: When to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the markedly different characteristics analysis only to nature-based product limitations in the claim to determine whether the nature-based products are "product of nature" exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a nature-based product can be claimed by itself or as one or more limitations of a claim, care should be taken not to overly extend the analysis to products that when viewed as a whole are not nature-based. If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, there is no need to perform the analysis because the limitation is directed to a naturally occurring product and thus falls under the product of nature exception. However, if the nature-based product limitation is not naturally occurring (e.g., due to some human intervention), then the markedly different characteristics analysis must be performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome rule for claims that include nature-based products with marked differences
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim includes a nature-based product that has markedly different characteristics, then the claim does not recite a product of nature exception and is eligible (Step 2A: NO) at Pathway B unless the claim recites another exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims where the entire claim is a single nature-based product, once a markedly different characteristic is shown, no further eligibility analysis is necessary (Step 2B is not necessary because the answer to Step 2A is NO). For claims including additional limitations, examiners should consider whether the claim recites another exception and thus requires further eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claim is to a nature-based product by itself, apply the markedly different characteristics analysis to the entire product; when the claim is to a nature-based combination, apply the analysis to the resultant combination; when combined with non-nature elements, apply only to the nature-based product limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: for a claim to "a Lactobacillus bacterium" analyze the whole bacterium; for a probiotic composition comprising Lactobacillus and milk, analyze the mixture as the resultant nature-based combination rather than components separately; for a yogurt starter kit comprising Lactobacillus in a container with instructions, analyze only the Lactobacillus for markedly different characteristics while the container/instructions are evaluated as additional elements in Prong Two (and Step 2B if needed). See Funk Bros. Seed Co. v. Kalo Inoculant Co. for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For product-by-process claims, the analysis turns on whether the nature-based product in the claim has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2113 for more information on product-by-process claims. The key is comparison of the claimed product (regardless of how it is made) to the naturally occurring counterpart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, process claims are not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products used in the process because process analysis focuses on active steps, not products used in those steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where the markedly different analysis is not applied: claims to cryopreserving hepatocyte cells were not subjected to the analysis for the hepatocytes used in the process (Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect). Exception: if a process claim is drafted such that it is no different in substance from a product claim (i.e., focuses on the product), it is subject to the markedly different analysis (e.g., a claim that recites "a method of providing an apple" or claims effectively to detecting naturally occurring cffDNA because they are directed to the product).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step is selecting the appropriate counterpart(s) to the nature-based product: the comparison must be to the naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nature-based product is derived from a naturally occurring thing, that natural thing is the counterpart (e.g., deoxyacid A -> acid A). Do not confuse the counterpart with other naturally associated material (e.g., compare an isolated gene to the gene, not the whole chromosome). When multiple counterparts exist, compare to the closest naturally occurring counterpart based on examiner expertise; for mixtures with no counterpart in nature, the closest counterparts may be the individual components. If the claim is rejected as ineligible, it is a best practice for the examiner to identify the selected counterpart in the Office action to clarify the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying appropriate characteristics for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify characteristics possessed by the claimed product (as defined by the claim language and its broadest reasonable interpretation) to compare with the counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate characteristics must be possessed by the claimed product; unclaimed characteristics cannot contribute to eligibility. Characteristics may be explicit in the claim (e.g., chemical name indicating structure) or inferred from the broadest reasonable interpretation (e.g., "isolated gene B" implies sequence and encoded protein). Characteristics can be expressed as structure, function, and/or other properties and are evaluated case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of characteristics to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting types of characteristics courts consider include biological/pharmacological functions or activities, chemical and physical properties, phenotype (functional and structural characteristics), and structure and form (chemical, genetic, or physical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: biological/pharmacological (protein-encoding information of a nucleic acid; complementary nucleotide binding; bacterial infectivity; hydrocarbon degradation; vitamin C preventing scurvy); chemical/physical (alkalinity; ductility/malleability); phenotype (shape, size, color, behavior); structure/form (physical presence of plasmids; chemical being a nonsalt/crystalline; nucleotide sequence; genotype). Use these categories to guide what to compare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating whether characteristics are "markedly different"
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the claimed product's characteristics to the naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state to determine whether they are "markedly different."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show a marked difference, a characteristic must be changed as compared to nature and cannot be an inherent or innate characteristic of the naturally occurring counterpart or an incidental change. The inventor must have caused the claimed product to possess at least one characteristic that is different from that of the counterpart. If there is no change in any characteristic, the claimed product is a product of nature exception. If there is a change in at least one characteristic and the change was produced by the inventor's efforts, the change will generally be considered a markedly different characteristic and the claimed product is not a product of nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative examples of products having markedly different characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Case examples where courts found markedly different characteristics and eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chakrabarty: genetically modified bacterium with additional plasmids and the ability to degrade multiple hydrocarbons was "markedly different" and eligible. Myriad: full-length cDNA (exons only) was structurally distinct from genomic DNA and found not a product of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative examples of products lacking markedly different characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Case examples where courts found products lacked marked differences and were product-of-nature exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myriad: isolated but otherwise unchanged genes (incidental isolation differences) were not markedly different. Ambry Genetics: primers with same nucleotide sequence and innate binding function were products of nature. In re Marden: ductility/malleability as inherent characteristic of vanadium was not a marked difference. Roslin: cloned farm animals that were genetic replicas lacked markedly different characteristics. Use these examples to identify anti-patterns (innate, incidental, or unclaimed differences do not qualify).
